findings.issue_text: [BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test cannot exercise the permDenialCache hit path because it seeds the denial key with parent 'fold1' but sends 'fold1' as the Folder field, so Check builds userPermDenialCacheKey with checkReq.ParentFolder == "" and misses. The test passes via the permCache fallback ({"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}) rather than the denial-cache short-circuit, so the new denial fast path ships with zero coverage; a regression in the denial-hit branch (e.g., returning allowed=true on hit) would not be caught by CI.

[BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey omits checkReq.Folder while checkPermission evaluates folder-scoped permissions, so a denial computed for one folder is served from cache for checks against a different folder with the same resource name and empty ParentFolder. A user denied dashboards:read on dash1 in folder A (e.g., permission scoped to folders:uid:foldA) gets a cached denial under key '..._dash1_'; a subsequent check on dash1 in folder B, where the user does have access, short-circuits to Allowed:false until the TTL expires — an authorization decision contradicted by fresh evaluation.

[ADVISORY] permDenialCache is written on every denial but is not wired into any cache-invalidation path, unlike the existing permission caches that other Grafana subsystems invalidate on permission changes. When a permission grant reaches the service through whatever invalidation mechanism exists for permCache today, the corresponding denial entries survive for shortCacheTTL, so users granted access keep getting denied up to the TTL with no way for callers to clear the stale deny.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type dispatch and cache-key construction of getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions as a second hand-maintained copy of the same type switch. The next identity type or key-format change must be applied in two places; drift already shows (the cached variant returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService while the uncached path has its own handling), and a future divergence silently changes which identities get cache hits vs. always pay the DB round-trip.

[ADVISORY] When getCachedIdentityPermissions fails for a reason other than cache.ErrNotFound (e.g., GetUserIdentifiers error), Check silently falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which repeats the same GetUserIdentifiers lookup and will fail again, doubling the failure cost. Every failing identity-resolution call on the Check hot path performs the store round-trip twice before returning the error; under a store outage this doubles load precisely when the store is already degraded.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is never invalidated anywhere in the diff, so a user who is denied once is served a cached denial for the full shortCacheTTL even after an administrator grants them the permission. After a permission grant (role/permission change), subsequent Check calls for the same (user, action, name, parent) hit the denial-cache branch at line 117 and return Allowed=false without consulting the store, so the grant does not take effect until the TTL expires — a correctness regression for permission changes that the permCache (positive cache) mitigates by falling back to the DB on stale data, but the denial cache has no such fallback.

[BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.ParentFolder but ignores checkReq.Folder, so a denial evaluated against one Folder is cached under a key shared by requests with different Folder values. A Check denied for name=dash1 with Folder=foldA (ParentFolder empty or equal) writes a denial entry; a later Check for the same name/action/parent but a different Folder value hits that denial entry and returns Allowed=false without evaluation — a cross-folder false denial. The test at service_test.go line ~960 only exercises the ParentFolder/Folder-equal case, hiding this.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch of getIdentityPermissions as a parallel hand-maintained enumeration, with TypeRenderService hardcoded to return cache.ErrNotFound. The next identity type added (or a change to how render-service identities are keyed) must be updated in both switches; missing the cached copy silently disables caching for that identity type, and the render-service branch sends every render check to the database with no cache read at all — the person bitten is whoever adds the next identity type or debugs render-service DB load.

[ADVISORY] The new tests cover only cache-hit allow, cache-miss allow, and explicit denial-cache entries; there is no test for the denial-cache staleness path (deny cached, then permission granted — which currently returns the stale denial) nor for getCachedIdentityPermissions' anonymous and render-service branches. The untested staleness behavior is exactly the P1 above: a regression in invalidation semantics or a future fix to the denial key cannot be caught by this suite, and the anonymous/render-service cache branches (service.go lines ~347-352) have zero coverage so a mistake there ships silently.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but the diff contains no invalidation path anywhere, so a permission granted to a user continues to be denied from cache until shortCacheTTL expires. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (e.g. adds a dashboard permission), subsequent Checks for that exact resource return Allowed=false from the denial cache for the full short TTL with no store round-trip, so the user's newly granted access does not take effect; under-scoping: the diff adds a new negative cache without the corresponding invalidation hook required to make it correct.

[ADVISORY] When cached permissions are found but checkPermission returns false, Check unconditionally re-fetches permissions from the store via getIdentityPermissions and re-runs the permission check, doing the same work twice on every cached-deny request. Every denied check that has a cached permission set (the common case for users without access) triggers a full database permission fetch plus a second checkPermission evaluation, so the 'cache' path costs a DB query for denials — the exact load the caching change was meant to remove; also the denial cache Set at line 150-153 then records the denial, meaning subsequent identical requests skip the DB but the first one pays double.

[ADVISORY] When cached permissions hit but the decision is deny, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with label "false" even though the cache was in fact used, corrupting the cache-hit-rate metric. Operators reading the permissionCacheUsage metric to evaluate whether this caching change works will see hit rates that undercount hits by the volume of cached-deny requests (all of which fall through to DB and re-increment as misses), making the feature's own success unmeasurable from the metrics it emits.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions re-implements the identity-type dispatch (anonymous key, user/service-account identifier lookup, render-service special case) that already exists in getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, creating a parallel hand-maintained enumeration with no single source of truth. The next identity-type change (e.g. adding a new TypeID or changing identifier resolution) must be applied in three places — getIdentityPermissions, getCachedIdentityPermissions, and the key builders — and missing one silently yields cache.ErrNotFound (cache bypass) or a wrong key collision rather than a compile error; drift is already visible in that the cached path returns ErrNotFound for render-service while the uncached path handles it elsewhere.

[ADVISORY] newRemoteRBACClient still configures a 30-second client-level local cache on top of the service-level permCache/permDenialCache added in this diff, leaving two independent caches with different TTLs and no shared invalidation on the remote path. On the remote-server deployment mode a permission change must now expire from both the client cache (30s) and the service caches (shortCacheTTL) before taking effect, and the denial cache added here cannot be invalidated through the client cache's key space at all, so the remote path inherits the stale-denial window with one extra layer on top.

[ADVISORY] The denial-cache lookup path returns early without consulting the permission cache or store, so a poisoned or stale denial entry for a shared key (anonymous userUID is empty in the key builder) denies an entire namespace/action for all anonymous users from one bad write. userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' separators and no escaping; for anonymous checks userUID is empty, so one denied anonymous check pins a denial entry that short-circuits every subsequent anonymous Check for that resource for the TTL, and an empty Name/ParentFolder in one request shape collides with a differently-shaped request for the same resource.

[ADVISORY] The new tests cover only the user/service-account happy paths of the cache; the anonymous branch of getCachedIdentityPermissions, the render-service bypass branch, and the checkPermission-error-on-cached-perms path in Check have no test coverage in this diff. A regression in the anonymous cached-permission branch (e.g. returning the wrong key or always ErrNotFound) would silently disable caching for all anonymous traffic, the largest request volume in most Grafana deployments, and no test in this diff would fail.

[BUG] The denial cache key is built from the raw request UserUID while the allow-cache path keys on the resolved store.UserIdentifiers.UID, so the two caches bind different identities for the same request. When GetUserIdentifiers resolves the request identity to a different canonical UID (or when a user and a service account share a UID in a namespace), a cached denial keyed on the raw UserUID denies an identity whose resolved permission cache would allow, or fails to deny the identity that was actually checked — denials and allows disagree for the same principal depending on which cache answers first.

[BUG] permDenialCache entries are written on every denial but no code path in the diff ever Deletes them, so denial survival after a permission grant depends solely on TTL expiry. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (the same event that invalidates permCache), the negative-cache entry for that exact resource/user/action pair survives and keeps returning Allowed:false until shortCacheTTL lapses; any existing invalidation hook that flushes permCache on role/permission change has no counterpart for permDenialCache, so grants take effect inconsistently between the two caches.

[BUG] The denial cache key has per-resource cardinality (namespace+user+action+name+parent), so a local cache that previously held O(users x actions) perm entries now materializes one entry per denied (user, resource, folder) tuple. A user browsing/listing many dashboards they cannot access (the common case for a locked-down viewer) inserts one cache entry per checked resource; on a busy instance the shared local cache fills with high-cardinality denial keys, evicting the lower-cardinality idCache/permCache/teamCache entries that actually prevent DB round-trips, degrading the very hit rate this change is meant to improve.

[ADVISORY] The cache-hit denial path increments requestCount with label values ("false", "true") — the same pair used for the allowed response — while returning Allowed:false, so the second label does not encode the response's actual outcome on this path. Anyone building dashboards or alerts on requestCount's allowed/denied dimension will undercount denials whenever the denial comes from the new negative cache, and the metric's meaning now varies by code path (DB-path denials flow through the final return with a different labeling pattern), making the series unreliable after this change.

[ADVISORY] On a cached-permission miss-to-deny, Check now resolves GetUserIdentifiers twice and runs checkPermission twice (once on cached perms, once on freshly fetched perms) before caching the denial. Every denied check on a warm-but-denying permCache pays an extra identity resolution plus a full re-evaluation instead of trusting the cache, doubling per-denied-check work for principals with no access — the population the negative cache was presumably built to serve fast; a single evaluation order (deny-cache → cached perms → DB once) would remove the duplicate path.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions' TypeAnonymous and TypeRenderService branches, and the deny-cache-precedes-identity-resolution ordering, are new non-trivial logic exercised only indirectly by the new tests, which cover only the TypeUser path with a pre-seeded idCache. A regression in the anonymous branch (e.g., anonPermCacheKey key mismatch with the writer in getAnonymousPermissions) or in denial-cache behavior for anonymous/RenderService identities would ship green: no test in the diff sends a Check or List for TypeAnonymous or TypeRenderService, and none exercises a denial written by the Check path (the deny test hand-seeds the cache instead), so the write-key/read-key pairing of userPermDenialCacheKey is never verified end-to-end.

[BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test populates the denial cache with parent 'fold1' but sends the Check request with Folder: 'fold1' and no ParentFolder, so userPermDenialCacheKey produces 'org-12.perm_test-uid_dashboards:read_dash1_' in Check while the seeded key is '...dash1_fold1' and the denial-cache lookup misses. The test asserts Allowed=false only because the pre-seeded permCache entry maps dash1 to false, so it passes vacuously and the denial-cache hit path is never actually exercised; a regression in the denial-cache lookup would go undetected.

[ADVISORY] The in-process client silently drops its 30s LocalCache (previously via newRBACClient) in favor of NoopCache while newRemoteRBACClient retains the 30s cache, changing per-Check behavior for all embedded callers without any test or explicit note in this diff. Every in-process Check now incurs a gRPC round-trip to the local server, shifting load onto the server-side Check path; anyone auditing cache behavior by client type sees two divergent cache policies with no documented rationale, and a future regression here is easy to miss.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getUserPermissions (anonymous key construction, render-service exclusion, user-identifier resolution) as a second hand-maintained copy. When identity-type handling changes (e.g., a new identity type or a change to identifier resolution), the two switches must be updated in lockstep; a missed update means the cached read path and the DB read path disagree about which identities are supported, producing inconsistent cache/DB behavior for that type.

[ADVISORY] The denial cache entry written on a DB-path denial is never invalidated or refreshed when the user's permissions later grant access, so grant latency for a previously-denied specific resource is bounded only by shortCacheTTL rather than by permission-change events. After an admin grants a user access to a specific dashboard, that user keeps receiving Allowed=false from permDenialCache until the TTL expires even if the permission cache has already refreshed with the grant — a window where the two caches disagree and the stricter (deny) one wins because the denial check runs first.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers the denial-cache lifecycle beyond the vacuous deny case: nothing asserts that a denial is written after a DB-path denial, that a grant becomes visible after TTL expiry, or that the anonymous/render-service branches of getCachedIdentityPermissions behave correctly. The newest, most subtle cache (permDenialCache) — the core of the PR's stated intent — can regress (wrong key shape, wrong TTL, deny-storm behavior) without any failing test, and the anonymous denial key with an empty userUID is never exercised.

[BUG] A denial is pinned in permDenialCache for the full shortCacheTTL with no invalidation path and no DB fallback, while the allow path falls back to the database whenever the cached permission map lacks the requested resource — an asymmetry where denials are served without revalidation but allows are rechecked. A user who is granted a role/permission continues to be denied access to that resource for up to shortCacheTTL (cache wrap TTL) with no cache-invalidation hook to clear the denial entry, so RBAC changes propagate asymmetrically: grants take effect late for specific resources while the underlying allow cache falls through to the database on resource miss (service.go:118-133). Nothing in this diff wires Delete() on permission changes, so the denial outlives the grant.

[ADVISORY] The denial-cache hit path increments permissionCacheUsage with label 'true' and requestCount with cached='false', denying='true', misreporting which layer served the request. Metrics consumers evaluating cache effectiveness for this change will undercount client-layer cache hits and misattribute denial-cache hits as fresh permission evaluations, corrupting the rollout signals used to judge whether the new caching layer is working.

[BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test cannot distinguish the permDenialCache short-circuit from an ordinary permCache denial: it also seeds s.permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, so checkPermission on the cached perms denies the same request, meaning the test passes even if the new permDenialCache.Get early-return in Service.Check is deleted entirely. False confidence: the only test claiming to verify the new denial-cache read path in fact verifies pre-existing cached-permission denial; a regression that removes or breaks the denial-cache lookup ships green.

[ADVISORY] No test exercises the denial-cache write path's downstream effect: a request denied and cached, followed by a re-Check after the underlying permission is granted (or after TTL expiry), verifying whether the stale denial is served. The riskiest behavior of the new cache — poisoned denials persisting up to shortCacheTTL and overriding fresh DB grants — is unverified; the 'outdated cache' subtest only covers stale allow-data, never stale deny-data, which is the direction where a regression silently locks users out.

[ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for types.TypeAnonymous, types.TypeRenderService, and the default unsupported-identity-type error have no test coverage anywhere in the diff (checked pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go — only TypeUser paths are exercised via TestService_CacheCheck/TestService_CacheList). The anonymous-permission cache-read branch (a hot path for unauthenticated traffic) and the unsupported-type error path can regress — e.g. returning nil perms with nil error instead of ErrNotFound, which would make Check evaluate an empty permission set and deny — without any test failing.

[ADVISORY] TestService_CacheList asserts the cached-hit happy path with concrete content (good), but never asserts the permissionCacheUsage metric or that the store was NOT hit, so it cannot detect that List silently fell through to the DB and still returned correct results. A regression where the cache read always misses (e.g. wrong key construction in getCachedIdentityPermissions) passes the suite because the DB fallback produces the identical response; the cache feature would be dead code in production while tests stay green.

[BUG] The permission-denial cache is short-circuited ahead of the allow path and is never invalidated on permission/role changes, so a denial persists for the full shortCacheTTL even after the underlying permission is granted. Once a check denies (including a transient deny from incomplete data such as a not-yet-synced team or folder relation), the permDenialCache.Set on the !allowed branch commits the denial; subsequent checks return Allowed:false at line 118-122 before the permCache allow path is ever consulted (the new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' explicitly proves the allow path is skipped). Any existing cache-invalidation logic for grants targets permCache keys only, so a newly granted permission keeps returning deny for up to shortCacheTTL with no way to flush it — users see access lag behind grants, and because the deny short-circuit bypasses permCache entirely, it cannot be corrected by a permCache refresh.

[BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unescaped fields with '_' and omits identity type, so distinct (action, name, parent, identityType) tuples can map to the same cache key and one subject's denial is served for another request. A name or parent containing '_' (e.g. name="dash_x", parent="" vs name="dash", parent="x") collides with a different check's key, and a user and a service account sharing a UID in the same namespace share the same key even though getIdentityPermissions dispatches on IdentityType — the cached denial from one identity/one resource is returned as an authorization decision for a different resource or identity type, producing wrong deny decisions that persist for the cache TTL.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication.rationale: The new denial-cache short-circuit is only taken if `s.permDenialCache.Get(ctx, permDenialKey)` hits, otherwise `Check` falls through to DB (`getIdentityPermissions` → `checkPermission`) and can still return `Allowed: false`. In `TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"`, the assertion is only `assert.False(t, resp.Allowed)`; it does not verify that the denial-cache branch executed (e.g., by ensuring the store is not called, checking metrics, or checking that a mismatched key would fail). Given the control flow in `Check`, this test could pass even if the denial-hit branch were broken, so it doesn’t guarantee coverage of the new fast path. The specific claim about `Folder` vs `ParentFolder` depends on parsing not shown in the diff, so that part can’t be conclusively verified here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey omits checkReq.Folder while checkPermission evaluates folder-scoped permissions, so a denial computed for one folder is served from cache for checks against a different folder with the same resource name and empty ParentFolder. adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `permDenialKey` is built with `checkReq.Name` **and** `checkReq.ParentFolder` (via `userPermDenialCacheKey(..., name, parent)`), so the denial cache key is already scoped by a folder-related field. Also, the newly added test `TestService_CacheCheck/Should deny on explicit cache deny entry` seeds `permDenialCache` with `userPermDenialCacheKey(..., "dash1", "fold1")` and then calls `Check` with `Folder: "fold1"`; this test would not pass if `checkReq.ParentFolder` were empty or unrelated to the request’s folder. From the diff alone, the claim that the key “omits checkReq.Folder” and causes cross-folder denial leakage is not supported.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] permDenialCache is written on every denial but is not wired into any cache-invalidation path, unlike the existing permission caches that other Grafana subsystems invalidate on permission changes. When a permission grant reaches the service through whatever invalidation mechanism exists for permCache today, the corresponding denial entries survive for shortCacheTTL, so users granted access keep getting denied up to the TTL with no way for callers to clear the stale deny.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial is now cached via `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` when `!allowed` (service.go), and future requests short-circuit to `Allowed: false` if `permDenialCache.Get` hits (before any permission recomputation) (service.go). The diff adds no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation/overwrite of these denial entries anywhere, so a previously-denied `(namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder)` can remain denied until `shortCacheTTL` even if underlying permissions change during that window.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type dispatch and cache-key construction of getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions as a second hand-maintained copy of the same type switch. The next identity type or key-format change must be applied in two places; drift already shows (the cached variant returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService while the uncached path has its own handling), and a future divergence silently changes which identities get cache hits vs. always pay the DB round-trip.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` with its own `switch idType` and cache-key construction (`anonymousPermCacheKey`, `GetUserIdentifiers` + `userPermCacheKey`) while the non-cached path still exists via `getIdentityPermissions(...)`/`getUserPermissions(...)`/`getAnonymousPermissions(...)`. Even within this diff, cache-related logic was moved out of `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` into this new function (removing prior cache checks), meaning identity-type dispatch and key formats are now maintained in at least two places (the cached dispatcher and the uncached permission-fetch path). That’s a concrete maintainability/drift risk created by the change, but not a verifiable functional defect from the shown code alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When getCachedIdentityPermissions fails for a reason other than cache.ErrNotFound (e.g., GetUserIdentifiers error), Check silently falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which repeats the same GetUserIdentifiers lookup and will fail again, doubling the failure cost. Every failing identity-resolution call on the Check hot path performs the store round-trip twice before returning the error; under a store outage this doubles load precisely when the store is already degraded.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new logic calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` and only treats the cache-hit path when `err == nil`. Any other error (including `GetUserIdentifiers` failing inside `getCachedIdentityPermissions` for user/service-account identities) is ignored and the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions(...)`, which for those identity types will call `GetUserIdentifiers` again (via `getUserPermissions`). This duplicates the identity-resolution/store work on the hot path during failures/outages, increasing load, but does not change correctness of the final allow/deny decision.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is never invalidated anywhere in the diff, so a user who is denied once is served a cached denial for the full shortCacheTTL even after an administrator grants them the permission. After a permission grant (role/permission change), subsequent Check calls for the same (user, action, name, parent) hit the denial-cache branch at line 117 and return Allowed=false without consulting the store, so the grant does not take effect until the TTL expires — a correctness regression for permission changes that the permCache (positive cache) mitigates by falling back to the DB on stale data, but the denial cache has no such fallback.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a cached denial is checked first and causes an immediate `Allowed: false` return (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). Later, any store-backed denial is written into this cache (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }`). The diff shows no invalidation/clearing of `permDenialCache` on permission/role changes, and the early-return means it will not consult the DB (or even the positive-permissions cache) for that `(namespace,user,action,name,parent)` tuple until TTL expiry, so a subsequent permission grant can be incorrectly denied during `shortCacheTTL`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.ParentFolder but ignores checkReq.Folder, so a denial evaluated against one Folder is cached under a key shared by requests with different Folder values. A Check denied for name=dash1 with Folder=foldA (ParentFolder empty or equal) writes a denial entry; a later Check for the same name/action/parent but a different Folder value hits that denial entry and returns Allowed=false without evaluation — a cross-folder false denial. The test at service_test.go line ~960 only exercises the ParentFolder/Folder-equal case, hiding this.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the denial cache key is explicitly computed from `checkReq.Name` and `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)`), and the helper `userPermDenialCacheKey`’s last parameter is named `parent` (used to build the key). There is no evidence in this diff that `checkReq` even has a separate `Folder` field distinct from `ParentFolder`, nor any mapping showing that `req.Folder` and `checkReq.ParentFolder` can diverge. The new test passes `CheckRequest{Folder: "fold1"}` and seeds the denial cache with `...parent="fold1"`, which is consistent with `req.Folder` being mapped into `checkReq.ParentFolder`. The claimed cross-folder false denial scenario depends on unshown behavior/fields and isn’t verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch of getIdentityPermissions as a parallel hand-maintained enumeration, with TypeRenderService hardcoded to return cache.ErrNotFound. The next identity type added (or a change to how render-service identities are keyed) must be updated in both switches; missing the cached copy silently disables caching for that identity type, and the render-service branch sends every render check to the database with no cache read at all — the person bitten is whoever adds the next identity type or debugs render-service DB load.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with its own `switch idType` (TypeAnonymous/TypeRenderService/TypeUser+TypeServiceAccount/default). `Check`/`List` now call this first, then fall back to `getIdentityPermissions` on error. This does create a parallel, hand-maintained identity-type enumeration separate from `getIdentityPermissions` (which already routes by identity type), so adding/changing identity types requires updating both places or caching will be bypassed for that type. Also, `TypeRenderService` is explicitly hardcoded to `return nil, cache.ErrNotFound`, meaning render-service requests will always skip the cache path and go to the DB fallback. This is a real maintainability/perf concern introduced by the change, but not a directly provable correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new tests cover only cache-hit allow, cache-miss allow, and explicit denial-cache entries; there is no test for the denial-cache staleness path (deny cached, then permission granted — which currently returns the stale denial) nor for getCachedIdentityPermissions' anonymous and render-service branches. The untested staleness behavior is exactly the P1 above: a regression in invalidation semantics or a future fix to the denial key cannot be caught by this suite, and the anonymous/render-service cache branches (service.go lines ~347-352) have zero coverage so a mistake there ships silently.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new caching logic paths that are only partially covered by the new tests. In `Service.Check`, an early-return denial is introduced via `permDenialCache` (service.go: `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`), but the added tests only cover a direct denial-cache hit (`TestService_CacheCheck/Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`) and do not exercise a “stale deny” scenario where the denial key remains while underlying permissions would allow. Separately, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` adds explicit branches for `types.TypeAnonymous` and `types.TypeRenderService` (service.go around the new switch), but the added tests only exercise the user path (cache hit/miss/outdated for a user subject) and do not cover anonymous or render-service behavior at all. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap for newly added logic rather than a directly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but the diff contains no invalidation path anywhere, so a permission granted to a user continues to be denied from cache until shortCacheTTL expires. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (e.g. adds a dashboard permission), subsequent Checks for that exact resource return Allowed=false from the denial cache for the full short TTL with no store round-trip, so the user's newly granted access does not take effect; under-scoping: the diff adds a new negative cache without the corresponding invalidation hook required to make it correct.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a deny is negatively cached via `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` and future checks short-circuit to `Allowed: false` on any cache hit (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return &CheckResponse{Allowed:false} }`) without consulting the permission store. The diff shows no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation call for `permDenialCache` (only `Get`/`Set` are used), so if permissions are later granted in the underlying store, the same (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) check will continue to be denied until the TTL expires.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When cached permissions are found but checkPermission returns false, Check unconditionally re-fetches permissions from the store via getIdentityPermissions and re-runs the permission check, doing the same work twice on every cached-deny request. Every denied check that has a cached permission set (the common case for users without access) triggers a full database permission fetch plus a second checkPermission evaluation, so the 'cache' path costs a DB query for denials — the exact load the caching change was meant to remove; also the denial cache Set at line 150-153 then records the denial, meaning subsequent identical requests skip the DB but the first one pays double.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new cache path returns early only on cached allow: it calls getCachedIdentityPermissions(...) and then checkPermission(...); if allowed is false, it always falls through to getIdentityPermissions(...) (DB-backed) and re-runs checkPermission on the fresh permissions (see the block added around lines ~113-146). That means a cached-deny (i.e., cached perms exist but don’t include the requested scope) still triggers a full permission fetch, so caching doesn’t reduce DB load for denials until after the DB-backed denial is recorded into permDenialCache (set only after the DB check at ~150-153). This is a real, diff-grounded performance/behavior concern (extra DB work), but not a correctness defect because the fallback appears intentional to handle stale/incomplete cached permission sets.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When cached permissions hit but the decision is deny, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with label "false" even though the cache was in fact used, corrupting the cache-hit-rate metric. Operators reading the permissionCacheUsage metric to evaluate whether this caching change works will see hit rates that undercount hits by the volume of cached-deny requests (all of which fall through to DB and re-increment as misses), making the feature's own success unmeasurable from the metrics it emits.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, cached permissions are consulted via getCachedIdentityPermissions(); if that returns cachedPerms and checkPermission returns allowed==false, the code does not record a cache hit and instead falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()` (the unconditional increment after the cachedPerms block). This means requests that *did* use the cache (to compute a deny) are counted as "false" (miss) in permissionCacheUsage, which misrepresents cache usage/hit rate as described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions re-implements the identity-type dispatch (anonymous key, user/service-account identifier lookup, render-service special case) that already exists in getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, creating a parallel hand-maintained enumeration with no single source of truth. The next identity-type change (e.g. adding a new TypeID or changing identifier resolution) must be applied in three places — getIdentityPermissions, getCachedIdentityPermissions, and the key builders — and missing one silently yields cache.ErrNotFound (cache bypass) or a wrong key collision rather than a compile error; drift is already visible in that the cached path returns ErrNotFound for render-service while the uncached path handles it elsewhere.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` that contains its own `switch idType` dispatch (anonymous uses `anonymousPermCacheKey`, user/service-account calls `GetUserIdentifiers` then `userPermCacheKey`, render-service returns `cache.ErrNotFound`). This duplicates identity-type handling logic that already exists elsewhere (e.g., `getUserPermissions`, `getAnonymousPermissions`, and likely `getIdentityPermissions` which now calls these without doing cache checks). This creates parallel, hand-maintained identity-type enumerations and key construction paths in multiple places, increasing drift risk and making future identity-type changes require edits in several functions rather than one.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] newRemoteRBACClient still configures a 30-second client-level local cache on top of the service-level permCache/permDenialCache added in this diff, leaving two independent caches with different TTLs and no shared invalidation on the remote path. On the remote-server deployment mode a permission change must now expire from both the client cache (30s) and the service caches (shortCacheTTL) before taking effect, and the denial cache added here cannot be invalidated through the client cache's key space at all, so the remote path inherits the stale-denial window with one extra layer on top.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `newRemoteRBACClient` still builds an `authzlib.NewClient` with a client-side `cache.NewLocalCache` (Expiry: 30s) (`pkg/services/authz/rbac.go`), while the server-side `Service` now relies on its own caches (`permCache` and newly added `permDenialCache`, both using `shortCacheTTL`) (`pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go`). There is nothing in the diff indicating any shared invalidation or coordination between these caches, so the remote path does indeed have two independent cache layers with different TTLs. However, the exact impact on “permission change must now expire from both” depends on `authzlib` cache semantics, which are not shown in the diff, so it’s more of an architectural/staleness concern than a strictly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial-cache lookup path returns early without consulting the permission cache or store, so a poisoned or stale denial entry for a shared key (anonymous userUID is empty in the key builder) denies an entire namespace/action for all anonymous users from one bad write. userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' separators and no escaping; for anonymous checks userUID is empty, so one denied anonymous check pins a denial entry that short-circuits every subsequent anonymous Check for that resource for the TTL, and an empty Name/ParentFolder in one request shape collides with a differently-shaped request for the same resource.
matched_golden_ids: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate explicitly calls out that `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds keys by concatenating components with '_' and does no escaping, leading to collisions/ambiguity when components are empty (e.g., anonymous userUID, empty Name/ParentFolder) and potentially causing incorrect denial-cache hits that affect permissions. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment, with additional context about impact.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new tests cover only the user/service-account happy paths of the cache; the anonymous branch of getCachedIdentityPermissions, the render-service bypass branch, and the checkPermission-error-on-cached-perms path in Check have no test coverage in this diff. A regression in the anonymous cached-permission branch (e.g. returning the wrong key or always ErrNotFound) would silently disable caching for all anonymous traffic, the largest request volume in most Grafana deployments, and no test in this diff would fail.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new caching branches via `getCachedIdentityPermissions` in `service.go` (anonymous: `anonPermCacheKey` lookup; render-service: unconditional `cache.ErrNotFound`; default error) and adds an early-deny path via `permDenialCache` in `Check`. The newly added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) exercise only the user/service-account cache-hit and cache-miss flows by populating `idCache` + `permCache` with `userPermCacheKey(...)`. There are no tests in the diff that cover (1) the anonymous cache-hit branch in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` using `anonymousPermCacheKey`, (2) the render-service bypass branch (`types.TypeRenderService` returning `cache.ErrNotFound`), or (3) the `checkPermission` error path when using cached perms in `Check` (the `if err != nil { ... return deny, err }` block after `checkPermission`). This is a concrete, diff-grounded test gap rather than a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The denial cache key is built from the raw request UserUID while the allow-cache path keys on the resolved store.UserIdentifiers.UID, so the two caches bind different identities for the same request. When GetUserIdentifiers resolves the request identity to a different canonical UID (or when a user and a service account share a UID in a namespace), a cached denial keyed on the raw UserUID denies an identity whose resolved permission cache would allow, or fails to deny the identity that was actually checked — denials and allows disagree for the same principal depending on which cache answers first.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial-cache key is built with `checkReq.UserUID` directly: `userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, ...)`. But the allow/list permission cache path (`getCachedIdentityPermissions`) resolves the principal via `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` and then keys permissions by `userIdentifiers.UID` (`userPermCacheKey(ns.Value, userIdentifiers.UID, action)`). This diff therefore makes the two caches potentially refer to different identifiers for the same request, so a cached denial may not correspond to the same canonical identity used for cached permissions (or vice versa), causing inconsistent allow/deny outcomes depending on which cache hits first.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] permDenialCache entries are written on every denial but no code path in the diff ever Deletes them, so denial survival after a permission grant depends solely on TTL expiry. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (the same event that invalidates permCache), the negative-cache entry for that exact resource/user/action pair survives and keeps returning Allowed:false until shortCacheTTL lapses; any existing invalidation hook that flushes permCache on role/permission change has no counterpart for permDenialCache, so grants take effect inconsistently between the two caches.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial is cached via `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` when `allowed` is false (service.go). On subsequent requests, the very first logic path is `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`, which short-circuits before consulting `permCache` or the DB. The diff shows no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation path for `permDenialCache` (only `Get`/`Set` usage), so a later permission grant for the same user/action/resource can be masked until `shortCacheTTL` expires, yielding stale denies.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The denial cache key has per-resource cardinality (namespace+user+action+name+parent), so a local cache that previously held O(users x actions) perm entries now materializes one entry per denied (user, resource, folder) tuple. A user browsing/listing many dashboards they cannot access (the common case for a locked-down viewer) inserts one cache entry per checked resource; on a busy instance the shared local cache fills with high-cardinality denial keys, evicting the lower-cardinality idCache/permCache/teamCache entries that actually prevent DB round-trips, degrading the very hit rate this change is meant to improve.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `permDenialCache` keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` (see `cache.go`) and populates it on every denied `Check()` (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`), short-circuiting future checks when present. This is indeed per-(user, action, resource name, parent folder) cardinality, unlike the existing `permCache` keyed only by (namespace, user UID, action). Since `permDenialCache` uses the same underlying local cache as `idCache/permCache/teamCache/...` (constructed in `NewService` with the shared `cache`), it can plausibly increase cache pressure and evict more valuable low-cardinality entries, harming cache hit rate and increasing DB round-trips. However, this is a performance/capacity tradeoff concern rather than a directly verifiable correctness/security defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cache-hit denial path increments requestCount with label values ("false", "true") — the same pair used for the allowed response — while returning Allowed:false, so the second label does not encode the response's actual outcome on this path. Anyone building dashboards or alerts on requestCount's allowed/denied dimension will undercount denials whenever the denial comes from the new negative cache, and the metric's meaning now varies by code path (DB-path denials flow through the final return with a different labeling pattern), making the series unreliable after this change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show the negative-cache denial path increments `requestCount.WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)` while returning `Allowed: false` (in `Service.Check`). However, the finding’s core assertion—that the second label encodes the allow/deny outcome and that DB-path denials use a different labeling pattern—is not verifiable from the diff: the label names/semantics for `requestCount` are not shown, and the final DB-path return also increments `requestCount` with the same ("false","true") pair regardless of whether `allowed` is true or false. So the claimed undercounting/inconsistency specific to the new negative cache cannot be confirmed from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] On a cached-permission miss-to-deny, Check now resolves GetUserIdentifiers twice and runs checkPermission twice (once on cached perms, once on freshly fetched perms) before caching the denial. Every denied check on a warm-but-denying permCache pays an extra identity resolution plus a full re-evaluation instead of trusting the cache, doubling per-denied-check work for principals with no access — the population the negative cache was presumably built to serve fast; a single evaluation order (deny-cache → cached perms → DB once) would remove the duplicate path.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, after permDenialCache is consulted, the code calls getCachedIdentityPermissions(), which for user/serviceaccount identities calls s.GetUserIdentifiers() to form userPermCacheKey and may return cached perms (service.go: getCachedIdentityPermissions). If cached perms are found but checkPermission returns allowed==false, Check then proceeds to call getIdentityPermissions(), whose user path calls getUserPermissions(), which again calls s.GetUserIdentifiers() (service.go: getUserPermissions). The permission evaluation is also performed twice (checkPermission on cachedPerms, then later after fetching permissions from DB/store). This is a diff-grounded performance/efficiency concern, not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions' TypeAnonymous and TypeRenderService branches, and the deny-cache-precedes-identity-resolution ordering, are new non-trivial logic exercised only indirectly by the new tests, which cover only the TypeUser path with a pre-seeded idCache. A regression in the anonymous branch (e.g., anonPermCacheKey key mismatch with the writer in getAnonymousPermissions) or in denial-cache behavior for anonymous/RenderService identities would ship green: no test in the diff sends a Check or List for TypeAnonymous or TypeRenderService, and none exercises a denial written by the Check path (the deny test hand-seeds the cache instead), so the write-key/read-key pairing of userPermDenialCacheKey is never verified end-to-end.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new non-trivial cache logic that is not directly exercised end-to-end by the new tests: (1) getCachedIdentityPermissions introduces TypeAnonymous (reads anonymousPermCacheKey) and TypeRenderService (always ErrNotFound) branches in service.go, but the added tests (TestService_CacheCheck/TestService_CacheList) only send requests for a user subject with a pre-seeded idCache/permCache path. (2) The new deny-cache path in Check() reads permDenialCache before resolving identity/permissions, and writes permDenialCache via permDenialCache.Set(...) when !allowed, but the deny test only pre-seeds permDenialCache and does not verify that a denial produced by Check() is later read back with the same userPermDenialCacheKey(...) (write-key/read-key pairing). This is a concrete test gap tied to the new logic, not a demonstrable defect in the diff itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test populates the denial cache with parent 'fold1' but sends the Check request with Folder: 'fold1' and no ParentFolder, so userPermDenialCacheKey produces 'org-12.perm_test-uid_dashboards:read_dash1_' in Check while the seeded key is '...dash1_fold1' and the denial-cache lookup misses. The test asserts Allowed=false only because the pre-seeded permCache entry maps dash1 to false, so it passes vacuously and the denial-cache hit path is never actually exercised; a regression in the denial-cache lookup would go undetected.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial-cache key is built with `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.ParentFolder)`), while the test request populates `Folder: "fold1"` and does not set any `ParentFolder` field on the proto. From the diff alone we can’t confirm how `newCheckRequest` maps `req.Folder` into `checkReq.ParentFolder`, so the claimed key-mismatch is not fully verifiable. However, the test is still weak/vacuous as written: it seeds `permCache` with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` despite the comment saying it is allowing access, and the test asserts `Allowed == false`, which could be satisfied even if the denial-cache lookup path is broken (e.g., via cached false or DB fallback denial). Thus it does not reliably exercise/verify the new explicit denial-cache short-circuit behavior introduced in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The in-process client silently drops its 30s LocalCache (previously via newRBACClient) in favor of NoopCache while newRemoteRBACClient retains the 30s cache, changing per-Check behavior for all embedded callers without any test or explicit note in this diff. Every in-process Check now incurs a gRPC round-trip to the local server, shifting load onto the server-side Check path; anyone auditing cache behavior by client type sees two divergent cache policies with no documented rationale, and a future regression here is easy to miss.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows ProvideAuthZClient switched from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` (which used a 30s `cache.NewLocalCache` via `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(...)`) to `authzlib.NewClient(..., authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, effectively disabling client-side caching for in-process/embedded callers. Meanwhile `newRemoteRBACClient` still constructs an `authzlib.NewClient` with the 30s local cache. This creates two divergent client cache policies grounded in the code change, and no tests in this diff cover the client-side cache behavior change (new tests added are for server-side Service cache paths).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getUserPermissions (anonymous key construction, render-service exclusion, user-identifier resolution) as a second hand-maintained copy. When identity-type handling changes (e.g., a new identity type or a change to identifier resolution), the two switches must be updated in lockstep; a missed update means the cached read path and the DB read path disagree about which identities are supported, producing inconsistent cache/DB behavior for that type.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with its own `switch idType` (handling `TypeAnonymous`, `TypeRenderService`, `TypeUser`/`TypeServiceAccount`, default error) and duplicated logic for cache-key construction and `GetUserIdentifiers` resolution. The DB path still has separate identity-type handling via `getIdentityPermissions` (and its downstream `getAnonymousPermissions` / `getUserPermissions`). This creates two hand-maintained identity-type decision points that could diverge when new identity types or identifier-resolution rules are added, causing inconsistent cache-vs-DB behavior. This is a maintainability/architecture risk rather than a directly verifiable functional defect in the current diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial cache entry written on a DB-path denial is never invalidated or refreshed when the user's permissions later grant access, so grant latency for a previously-denied specific resource is bounded only by shortCacheTTL rather than by permission-change events. After an admin grants a user access to a specific dashboard, that user keeps receiving Allowed=false from permDenialCache until the TTL expires even if the permission cache has already refreshed with the grant — a window where the two caches disagree and the stricter (deny) one wins because the denial check runs first.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a hit in `permDenialCache` immediately returns `Allowed: false` before consulting `permCache` or the DB (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). The denial entry is written only on the DB path when `allowed` is false (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }`) and there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidating logic when a later check would be allowed. Therefore, if permissions change from deny->allow, the stale denial cache will continue to force-deny until `shortCacheTTL` expires, even if `permCache` (or DB) would now allow—exactly the disagreement window described in the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers the denial-cache lifecycle beyond the vacuous deny case: nothing asserts that a denial is written after a DB-path denial, that a grant becomes visible after TTL expiry, or that the anonymous/render-service branches of getCachedIdentityPermissions behave correctly. The newest, most subtle cache (permDenialCache) — the core of the PR's stated intent — can regress (wrong key shape, wrong TTL, deny-storm behavior) without any failing test, and the anonymous denial key with an empty userUID is never exercised.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new, nontrivial denial-cache behavior (Service.permDenialCache) and a new cached-permissions fast path (getCachedIdentityPermissions + early returns in Check/List). The added tests cover: (1) allow from permCache, (2) DB fallback on miss/outdated cache, and (3) deny when an explicit permDenialCache entry already exists. However, nothing in the diff’s tests asserts the new lifecycle behavior implemented in Check—i.e., that a DB-path denial triggers `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` (service.go), nor any TTL/expiry behavior, nor the anonymous (`TypeAnonymous`) and render-service (`TypeRenderService`) branches of `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (service.go) beyond returning ErrNotFound. This is a specific, diff-grounded missing-test gap for the newly added core cache logic, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] A denial is pinned in permDenialCache for the full shortCacheTTL with no invalidation path and no DB fallback, while the allow path falls back to the database whenever the cached permission map lacks the requested resource — an asymmetry where denials are served without revalidation but allows are rechecked. A user who is granted a role/permission continues to be denied access to that resource for up to shortCacheTTL (cache wrap TTL) with no cache-invalidation hook to clear the denial entry, so RBAC changes propagate asymmetrically: grants take effect late for specific resources while the underlying allow cache falls through to the database on resource miss (service.go:118-133). Nothing in this diff wires Delete() on permission changes, so the denial outlives the grant.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check(), a hit in permDenialCache immediately returns Allowed=false with no revalidation (service.go:115-121). Denial entries are created on any DB-evaluated deny (service.go:150-153) and kept for shortCacheTTL via cacheWrap, but this diff shows no invalidation hook being called to clear them on permission/role changes. By contrast, the allow-path consults permCache and, if the cached permission map doesn’t allow the specific resource, it falls through to a fresh DB permission fetch (service.go:123-147). This creates an asymmetry where newly granted permissions can be blocked until the denial TTL expires, even though the DB would now allow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial-cache hit path increments permissionCacheUsage with label 'true' and requestCount with cached='false', denying='true', misreporting which layer served the request. Metrics consumers evaluating cache effectiveness for this change will undercount client-layer cache hits and misattribute denial-cache hits as fresh permission evaluations, corrupting the rollout signals used to judge whether the new caching layer is working.

adjudication.rationale: In the denial-cache hit path (`Service.Check`), the code increments `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)` and `requestCount.WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)`. From the diff alone, there is no evidence that `requestCount`’s labels correspond to `cached` and `denying` (the same `("false","true")` tuple is also used on successful allow responses, while `("true","true")` is used on error paths, suggesting the first label is more likely an error/success flag). Also, counting a denial-cache hit as a cache hit in `permissionCacheUsage` is not demonstrably “misreporting” without the metric’s intended semantics, which are not shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test cannot distinguish the permDenialCache short-circuit from an ordinary permCache denial: it also seeds s.permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, so checkPermission on the cached perms denies the same request, meaning the test passes even if the new permDenialCache.Get early-return in Service.Check is deleted entirely. False confidence: the only test claiming to verify the new denial-cache read path in fact verifies pre-existing cached-permission denial; a regression that removes or breaks the denial-cache lookup ships green.
matched_golden_ids: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point out that the test seeds the normal permission cache with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` while the test/comment intends to rely on another mechanism (cached permissions/denial-cache) to drive the outcome. Because the regular cache already denies, `checkPermission` still treats the scope as not allowed, making the test/comment misleading and the test ineffective at validating the intended path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test exercises the denial-cache write path's downstream effect: a request denied and cached, followed by a re-Check after the underlying permission is granted (or after TTL expiry), verifying whether the stale denial is served. The riskiest behavior of the new cache — poisoned denials persisting up to shortCacheTTL and overriding fresh DB grants — is unverified; the 'outdated cache' subtest only covers stale allow-data, never stale deny-data, which is the direction where a regression silently locks users out.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `permDenialCache` that is written on DB denial (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`) and then short-circuits future `Check` calls to deny (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). Tests added cover (a) cached allow, (b) DB fallback on cache miss/outdated allow, and (c) an explicit pre-populated denial entry (`TestService_CacheCheck` "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"), but no test exercises the write-then-read behavior where a denial is cached by the service and later becomes stale relative to DB grants/TTL. That’s a specific, diff-grounded missing-test gap around the new denial-cache semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for types.TypeAnonymous, types.TypeRenderService, and the default unsupported-identity-type error have no test coverage anywhere in the diff (checked pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go — only TypeUser paths are exercised via TestService_CacheCheck/TestService_CacheList). The anonymous-permission cache-read branch (a hot path for unauthenticated traffic) and the unsupported-type error path can regress — e.g. returning nil perms with nil error instead of ErrNotFound, which would make Check evaluate an empty permission set and deny — without any test failing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new helper `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` with a `switch` over `types.IdentityType` (handling `TypeAnonymous`, `TypeRenderService`, `TypeUser/TypeServiceAccount`, and a `default` error). The only new tests added (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) create requests with `Subject: "user:test-uid"`, exercising the user path (and the new `permDenialCache` behavior), but nothing in the diff adds tests that drive `TypeAnonymous`, `TypeRenderService`, or the `default` unsupported-type branch. Since anonymous caching was moved out of `getAnonymousPermissions` (its cache-hit branch was removed) into this new helper, lack of coverage for the anonymous cache-read branch is a concrete, diff-grounded gap that could regress without failing tests. This is a missing-coverage issue rather than a provable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TestService_CacheList asserts the cached-hit happy path with concrete content (good), but never asserts the permissionCacheUsage metric or that the store was NOT hit, so it cannot detect that List silently fell through to the DB and still returned correct results. A regression where the cache read always misses (e.g. wrong key construction in getCachedIdentityPermissions) passes the suite because the DB fallback produces the identical response; the cache feature would be dead code in production while tests stay green.

adjudication.rationale: In the added TestService_CacheList, the test sets idCache/permCache and asserts only the returned Items/Folders. It does not assert that getCachedIdentityPermissions actually hit the cache (e.g., via permissionCacheUsage metrics) nor that s.permissionStore/s.store were not consulted. Given List() now explicitly falls back to s.getIdentityPermissions() on cache miss (service.go: List), this test would not catch a regression where the cache path is bypassed as long as the fallback returns the same data. The finding is a test-coverage/verification gap around newly added caching behavior, not a runtime correctness defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The permission-denial cache is short-circuited ahead of the allow path and is never invalidated on permission/role changes, so a denial persists for the full shortCacheTTL even after the underlying permission is granted. Once a check denies (including a transient deny from incomplete data such as a not-yet-synced team or folder relation), the permDenialCache.Set on the !allowed branch commits the denial; subsequent checks return Allowed:false at line 118-122 before the permCache allow path is ever consulted (the new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' explicitly proves the allow path is skipped). Any existing cache-invalidation logic for grants targets permCache keys only, so a newly granted permission keeps returning deny for up to shortCacheTTL with no way to flush it — users see access lag behind grants, and because the deny short-circuit bypasses permCache entirely, it cannot be corrected by a permCache refresh.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new permDenialCache is consulted first and hard-denies immediately on a cache hit (service.go: new block before getCachedIdentityPermissions). Denial entries are written whenever the computed result is !allowed (s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)). There is no logic in this diff to clear/overwrite a denial entry when permissions later become allowed (either via permCache hit or DB evaluation), so a previously cached denial will continue to return Allowed:false and will also override any subsequent cached allow because the deny check short-circuits before the allow path. This can cause incorrect denies for up to shortCacheTTL after permissions/roles change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unescaped fields with '_' and omits identity type, so distinct (action, name, parent, identityType) tuples can map to the same cache key and one subject's denial is served for another request. A name or parent containing '_' (e.g. name="dash_x", parent="" vs name="dash", parent="x") collides with a different check's key, and a user and a service account sharing a UID in the same namespace share the same key even though getIdentityPermissions dispatches on IdentityType — the cached denial from one identity/one resource is returned as an authorization decision for a different resource or identity type, producing wrong deny decisions that persist for the cache TTL.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` is implemented as simple string concatenation with `_` separators: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. In `Service.Check`, this key is consulted first (`permDenialCache.Get`) and immediately returns `Allowed: false` on a hit. Because the fields are not escaped/length-delimited, different `(action,name,parent)` tuples can produce the same key when `name`/`parent` contain underscores or are split differently. Also, the denial key does not include `IdentityType` (and is built from `checkReq.UserUID`), so a cached denial can be reused across different identity types if they share the same `UserUID` string within a namespace, even though later permission retrieval logic branches on `IdentityType`. Both issues can cause incorrect deny decisions to be served from cache for a different request.
